Bhavna,
After Sunday's long talk on the balcony, I wanted to write down where we landed, so neither of us remembers it more kindly than it was.
Where to live: we agree on Pune for at least three years, near your office. I said I might want Guwahati later, near my parents. You said "maybe", and I'm writing it down as a real maybe, not a yes.
Children: you want them; I'm unsure. We agreed we're not ready to decide, and that "unsure" is allowed to be an honest answer.
Parents: your mother still calls me "your friend". You said you'll talk to her yourself, not leave it to me.
Careers: I'm applying for the Mumbai fellowship. You were quiet, then said you'd rather know now than be surprised.
Money: joint account for rent and groceries, separate for everything else.
I'm glad we found the children question now, over chai, and not years from now.
Love, and questions,
Minakshi

You asked why we postponed the engagement, Suresh. It's not what you think. Nothing's wrong. Something's right, actually.
Gargi and I sat down one Sunday with a notebook, of all things. She'd said, "Before our families book a hall, let's talk about the boring stuff." So we did. Where we'd live. Whether I'd move to Hyderabad for her job, or she'd come to Mysuru. How often we'd visit my parents, because my mother expects every weekend. Children: when, and whether at all. Who handles money.
It got uncomfortable. I found out she doesn't want to live with my parents, ever. I'd always just assumed. We argued. Then we stopped arguing, because we started solving it.
Better to have that fight in a notebook now than across a wedding hall later. We'll fix a date once we've worked out the parents question. Honestly? Harsha trusts Gargi more now, not less.

"You're really sure?" Shalini asked, stirring her coffee in the little café near Lalremsiami's office in Bengaluru. "Joel forgets everything. He forgot your birthday dinner reservation."
Lalremsiami laughed. "He did. And he's messy, and he goes quiet when he's upset." She turned her ring. "I'm not marrying some perfect man, Shalini."

Class teacher's note, Class 10C, 14 August.
Over the past month Alka has started a relationship with Nikhil from 10A; it is common knowledge in the class. She seems very happy. She lights up when he passes the door, and I've seen them on the stairs for the whole lunch break, heads close over one phone.
At the same time, her maths homework has been late three times, and she told me she'd been "on a call till one". Jasleen, who used to eat with Alka every day, has been sitting alone near the water cooler. When I asked her, she shrugged: "Alka's busy."

Come here, Shalini. You think these phone troubles are new? In 1979, in Aizawl, I, Lalremsiami, was sixteen and Zothan was seventeen. We wrote notes and passed them through my cousin at church every Sunday.
At first his notes were two pages. Then one page. Then half a page, about football. I wrote longer and longer notes, asking what he was thinking, asking why he didn't come by the bakery any more.
Once he sent back one line: "You write too much, Siami." I was so angry I tore it up. But I still wrote him a long note the next week.
And here is the thing, my dear. Neither of us said, "Something has changed." I was afraid that if I said it, it would be true. I think he was afraid too.
So we both just waited. Waiting doesn't fix a crack. It only hides it.

Your Rajni bua was fifteen once, you know. There was a boy in my tuition, Vishal. For three months he was my whole world. Then, slowly, I got bored. Not of him exactly, but of the same phone calls every night, the same "what are you doing now?"

He didn't understand. He felt me slipping, so he called more. He waited outside tuition every day, even when I'd said I had to rush home. He sent me songs with sad lyrics. And every time he needed me more, I felt more trapped and pulled further away.
It was like a knot that tightens when you pull. I should have told him honestly what I felt. Instead we both spent a month going round and round.

In Ambur the tuition centre let out at six, and the street smelled of biryani and rain. Ayesha had asked Junaid to wait at the tea stall. Keerthana had walked with her halfway and squeezed her hand: "Short and kind. You practised."

Ayesha walked back to Keerthana on shaking legs. She didn't feel good. But she felt clean, as if she hadn't left a mess behind for him to sort out.

Beatriz had moved to Cape Town from São Paulo two years ago, and Lindiwe had been the first person to sit with her at lunch. They'd been together since March. By September, Beatriz knew her feelings had changed.
She didn't want to do it by text. On Sunday evening she called.
"Lindi, I have to say something, and I'm going to say it straight because you deserve that," she said, sitting on her bedroom floor. "I care about you a lot. But I don't feel the way I did, and I won't keep you hoping for something I can't give."

"No. Honestly, no. You've been nothing but good to me."
"Okay." A shaky breath. "I'm glad you called instead of just going quiet."

"The Berlin team replied," Mohit said, not looking up from his laptop. "They want a second interview."
"Oh. That's great." Sudha folded a kurta very carefully. "When?"
"Next Thursday."
"Great."
"You keep saying great."
"It is great. For you."
"For us, I hoped."
Sudha put the kurta down. "Mohit, my parents are getting older. Papa's knee. I told you I wanted to stay in Jaipur."
"I know. I just thought, maybe for two years..."
"Let's talk about it after the interview. No point before."
"Yeah. After."
He went back to the laptop. She went back to folding. Neither of them said what both were thinking: that "after" had been the answer for four months now.

I'm Reena, and I think I knew by last spring that Joseph and I were walking in different directions. I'd started volunteering at weekends with a school project in the Nilgiris, and every time I came back to Kochi I felt more awake. I wanted to go there full-time. Live simply. Teach.
Joseph's dream was the opposite: a flat near his parents in Kakkanad, a steady bank job, Sunday mass with his family. Good dreams. Just not mine.
We did talk about it, in a way. "Maybe someday," he'd say. "Let's see how things are next year," I'd say. Our talks about the future got shorter and more polite, like two people being careful in a shop.
Looking back, the silence wasn't peaceful. It was both of us afraid to ask the question that might have an answer we didn't want.

qa.q: Where had Reena been volunteering at weekends?
qa.a: Reena had been volunteering at weekends with a school project in the Nilgiris.

qa.q: What were Reena and Joseph afraid of as their talks got short and polite?
qa.a: Both were afraid to ask the big question in case the answer was one they didn't want.

qa.q: What could they do instead of 'maybe someday'?
qa.a: They could sit down and say plainly what each wants, the Nilgiris or Kakkanad, and ask whether a shared path exists, perhaps with help from someone they trust.

qa.q: How might Joseph see Reena's weekends in the Nilgiris?
qa.a: Joseph may see them as a hobby and hope Reena will settle in Kochi, not realising how strongly they are pulling Reena away.

grounding: Illustrates a couple diverging between a different way of life and stability near family, with future talks turning polite and postponed.
